title: Binary Search
description: Halve the search range on a sorted array. Closed interval [l, r] with `l <= r`.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm given a sorted array `nums` and a `target`, and I want to return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it's not present. A few things to confirm:"

• Sorted ascending — that's the precondition, right?
• Are values unique, or can there be duplicates? (For plain BS it doesn't change the search, but it does change what 'the' index even means.)
• If the target appears multiple times, do you want any matching index, the leftmost, or the rightmost?
• Empty array — return `-1`?
• Any value bounds I should know about (int range, floats)?
sections.why: The sortedness question sounds like overkill but I always ask — every BS bug story starts with somebody running it on an unsorted array. The leftmost/rightmost question is the one that signals 'I know this template generalizes to lower_bound/upper_bound,' which is the first thing a strong interviewer probes for after the basic version works.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is a linear scan: walk from index 0, return `i` when `nums[i] === target`, return `-1` if I fall off the end. That's O(n) time, O(1) space — and it doesn't use the sortedness at all, which is the giveaway that we can do better."
sections.why: Stating linear scan first does two things. (1) It confirms I read the prompt — I'm not assuming BS is the goal, I'm deriving it from 'O(n) ignores the structure I was given.' (2) It frames the optimization as 'exploit the order' rather than 'apply binary search,' which is the right mental motion — patterns come from properties, not labels.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What property of the input unlocks binary search?
sections.say:
"This is the canonical binary-search trigger: a sorted array gives me a monotone property — for any index `m`, every element left of `m` is `<= nums[m]`, and every element to the right is `>= nums[m]`. That monotonicity is what lets me discard half the search space in one comparison. So instead of one pass, I shrink the range by half each step: O(log n)."

"Two template choices worth flagging up front: I'll use a CLOSED interval `[l, r]` with `while (l <= r)` — the `=` matters, otherwise single-element ranges get skipped. And I'll move PAST `m` with `l = m + 1` / `r = m - 1` to guarantee the range shrinks every iteration; `l = m` is the classic infinite-loop trap."
sections.why: Naming the *property* — monotone order — separates BS from pattern-matching on the word 'sorted.' The closed-interval-and-move-past-m callouts are the two implementation choices interviewers grill on; saying them up front signals you've written this loop before and remember why each piece is the way it is, instead of fumbling them under pressure.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a couple of inputs to make sure the loop boundaries are right." Three cases cover the interesting behaviors — a hit deep in the array, a miss where the loop has to terminate cleanly, and a single-element array that exercises the `l <= r` boundary.

examples.trace:
l=0 r=5  m=2 nums[m]=3   < 9 → l = m+1 = 3
l=3 r=5  m=4 nums[m]=9   === 9 → return 4 ✓

examples.note: Miss — the loop must terminate via l > r, not loop forever.
examples.trace:
l=0 r=6  m=3 nums[m]=7   > 2 → r = m-1 = 2
l=0 r=2  m=1 nums[m]=3   > 2 → r = m-1 = 0
l=0 r=0  m=0 nums[m]=1   < 2 → l = m+1 = 1
l=1 r=0  → l > r, loop exits → return -1 ✓

examples.note: Single-element array — this is why `<=` matters, not `<`.
examples.trace:
l=0 r=0  → l <= r is TRUE (would be FALSE with `<`)
           m=0 nums[m]=5 === 5 → return 0 ✓

sections.why: The miss-case trace is the one to narrate slowly — it's where careless implementations infinite-loop (writing `l = m` instead of `l = m + 1`) or off-by-one (writing `l < r` instead of `l <= r` and missing the last comparison). The single-element trace is the cleanest way to defend the `<=` choice on the spot: 'with `<` this returns -1 instead of 0.' Both bugs are caught on the whiteboard, not in the runtime.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Empty array → `r = -1`, loop never enters, return `-1`. ✓
• Single element matching target → returns 0 only if the loop condition is `<=`. With `<` it returns -1. Already flagged.
• Target smaller than `nums[0]` or larger than `nums[n-1]` → the range collapses to one side and exits cleanly with -1.
• Duplicates → plain BS returns *some* index of `target`, not necessarily the first or last. If the interviewer wants leftmost, swap to the `lower_bound` template (`while (l < r)`, `if (nums[m] < target) l = m+1; else r = m;`).
• Integer overflow on `(l + r) / 2` → in JS, numbers are 64-bit floats so it's safe up to 2^53. In Java/C++ you'd write `l + ((r - l) >> 1)` to dodge `INT_MAX` overflow. Worth mentioning that you'd port it that way in a typed language.
sections.why: The overflow callout is the senior-tier flag — in JS it's a non-issue, but mentioning that you *would* protect it in C++/Java signals language-portability awareness. The duplicates callout is the bridge to the more advanced versions of this template (first/last occurrence, ceiling, floor) — naming `lower_bound` unprompted shows you see the family, not just this one instance.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(log n) — each iteration halves the search range, so after `k` steps the range is `n / 2^k`. The loop terminates when the range is empty, which happens at `k = log₂(n) + 1`. So worst case is `⌈log₂(n)⌉ + 1` comparisons.

Space is O(1) — just the three integer pointers, no recursion stack. If I wrote this recursively it would be O(log n) auxiliary space from the call stack, which is why I prefer the iterative form.

If you wanted to extend: the same `l/r/m` skeleton becomes `lower_bound` (first index >= target) by swapping the comparison and the loop condition, and from there you get insertion-point, ceiling, floor, and 'first/last occurrence of target' as one-line variants. That's the whole binary-search family from one template."
sections.why: The halving argument is the textbook defense, but the iterative-vs-recursive aside is what shows up-leveled engineering judgment — the asymptotic cost is the same but the constant factors and stack pressure differ. Naming `lower_bound` and the family of variants is the bonus that proves you see this as a *template*, not a one-off; that's the move that earns the 'strong hire' bullet on the rubric.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical binary search one statement at a time on a real sorted input. The highlighted line is what just ran; the state panel shows l, r, m, and nums[m] after that step.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — nums=${JSON.stringify(nums)}, target=${target}`, state: { nums, target } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init l=0, r=nums.length-1=${r}`, state: { nums, target, l, r } };
yield { line: 4, label: `loop check: l=${l} <= r=${r} → enter`, state: { nums, target, l, r } };
yield { line: 5, label: `m = floor((${l}+${r})/2) = ${m}, nums[m]=${nums[m]}`, state: { nums, target, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `nums[m]=${nums[m]} === target=${target} → return ${m}`, state: { nums, target, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m], returns: m } };
yield { line: 8, label: `nums[m]=${nums[m]} < target=${target} → l = m+1 = ${l}`, state: { nums, target, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m] } };
yield { line: 9, label: `nums[m]=${nums[m]} > target=${target} → r = m-1 = ${r}`, state: { nums, target, l, r, m, midVal: nums[m] } };
yield { line: 11, label: `loop ended (l=${l} > r=${r}) — target not found, return -1`, state: { nums, target, l, r, returns: -1 } };

notes: Array MUST be sorted — that’s the whole prerequisite.
Loop condition is `l <= r` because [l, r] is a CLOSED interval; missing `=` skips single-element ranges.
Move past m by +1/-1 to guarantee progress and avoid infinite loops.

Why O(log n)? Each iteration halves the search range. After k halvings, size = n / 2^k; loop ends when 2^k ≥ n, so k ≈ log₂(n). For the full derivation + contrast with O(1)/O(n)/O(n²), drill the `s-bigo-intuition` lesson.
reference.crux: Compare target to the midpoint and throw away the half it can't be in — sortedness makes one comparison eliminate half the candidates, giving O(log n).
cruxDistractors: Scan left to right and return the index the moment `nums[i] === target` — sortedness lets you stop early on a miss.
Jump in √n-sized blocks until you overshoot target, then linear-scan back through the last block.
Compare adjacent pairs and recurse into whichever side's endpoints bracket the target's value.

alternates.label: Recursive
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer specifically asks for the recursive formulation, or when you want to show you can express the same idea both ways. Prefer iterative in production — JS has no tail-call optimization, so every call adds an O(log n) stack frame.
notes: Same three-branch logic as iterative — base case, hit, recurse into the live half.
Default parameters `l = 0, r = nums.length - 1` make the public call site clean.
Space is O(log n) from the call stack — the iterative version's key advantage over this one.

options: `<` would let `m` go negative on the last iteration when the range shrinks
[l, r] is closed; without the equal you miss single-element ranges
`<` would terminate one step too late and re-check an already-discarded half
`<=` is required to correctly compute `Math.floor((l+r)/2)` when l === r

questions.q: If you write `l = m` instead of `l = m + 1`:
options: Returns the first occurrence of target instead of an arbitrary occurrence
Risk of infinite loop
Off-by-one — the returned index is one less than the true index of target
Loses the lower_bound property — l no longer points to the insertion point on a miss
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
O(sqrt(n))
Values must be distinct (no duplicates)
Must be sorted
Length must be a power of 2 so the halving is exact
Values must be non-negative

questions.q: With the closed interval `[l, r]`, what is the loop invariant — what stays true at the start of every iteration?
options: l and r are always different
If target is present, its index is within [l, r]
nums[l] is always less than target
m is always the answer
questions.explain: The interval [l, r] always still contains target if it exists; each step discards a half that provably cannot contain it.

questions.q: Why is `m = l + ((r - l) >> 1)` preferred over `m = (l + r) / 2` in fixed-width-integer languages like C++/Java?
options: `>>` is a single CPU instruction whereas `/` is multi-cycle, so the loop iterations are tighter
`l + r` can overflow INT_MAX even when both indices are valid; `l + (r-l)/2` cannot
It rounds toward zero on negative ranges, which matters when binary-searching answer-space below zero
It avoids the implicit float→int truncation that JIT compilers handle inconsistently across versions
questions.explain: For large l and r, l + r can exceed the int max and wrap negative; l + (r - l)/2 stays within range. (In JS, Numbers are 64-bit floats so it is only a portability concern.)

questions.q: Why is the algorithm guaranteed to terminate?
options: Because the array is finite
Because moving past m (l = m+1 / r = m-1) strictly shrinks [l, r] every iteration until l > r
Because target is always found
Because m eventually equals 0
questions.explain: Each non-returning step removes at least the element at m plus one half, so the interval strictly shrinks and the loop must end.

questions.q: After a FAILED search (target absent), what does `l` point to when the loop exits?
options: The last index checked
The insertion point — the index where target would be inserted to keep the array sorted
Always 0
Always nums.length
questions.explain: On exit l is the lower_bound: the leftmost index whose value is >= target, i.e. where target would go to keep order.

questions.q: Binary search is applicable whenever the input is exactly which of the following?
options: A sorted array only
Any data with a monotonic predicate — sortedness is one instance, but answer-space searches qualify too
Any array of numbers
Only arrays with unique values
questions.explain: The real requirement is a monotone yes/no boundary; a sorted array gives one, but so does any monotone feasibility predicate (e.g. binary search on the answer).
